results.note: Every number matches at the stated places: 74,601 and 298,404 (Findings 1st paragraph; also Study population 2nd paragraph); 1,722 / 367,696 / 4.68 and 1,144 / 1,487,536 / 0.77, crude 6.08 (5.64 to 6.55), adjusted 5.28 (4.90 to 5.70) (Table 2 All row; Findings 2nd paragraph); 3.75% vs 0.63% at the end of 10 years (Findings 2nd paragraph). Study population 1st paragraph gives the linkage, ages 18 or older, the urine tests, first arrest as index date, comparisons insured in the index year and four per exposed person frequency matched on index year, age and sex. Only one element sits outside the stated locator: the 1st paragraph excludes earlier psychosis for the comparisons only; the exclusion for all subjects, both cohorts, is in the 2nd paragraph, hence the locator correction. The adjustment set (age, sex, comorbidities) is in Findings 2nd paragraph and Table 2 footnote. The 10-year figures are Kaplan-Meier estimates with death treated as censoring. Role supports: right for an association claim (same direction).
results.corrected_locator: Methods › Study population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2, All row

results.note: All content is at the stated places: 23 substance names counted in Study population 1st paragraph (methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA among them; no breakdown anywhere); comorbidities diagnosed during 2007-2016 (3rd paragraph) and the adjustment set (Table 2 footnote †); the code lists and the included-diagnosis list naming other stimulant use disorders with psychosis (2nd paragraph); not preregistered, exploratory (Data source 2nd paragraph). The only change is precision: the anchor wrote '296.04–296.64', which reads as a range of all codes from 296.04 to 296.64 (including mood-disorder codes without psychotic features); the paper lists seven codes, each ending in 4, and the correction lists them. Role qualifies: right.
results.corrected_extracted: The 23 substances defining exposure include methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA; no breakdown by substance is given. Adjustment: age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses (depression, anxiety, ischaemic heart disease, cardiovascular disease, stroke) recorded at any time during 2007–2016; nothing for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position or family history. Outcome codes listed: 295, 296.04, 296.14, 296.24, 296.34, 296.44, 296.54 and 296.64 (mood disorders with psychotic features), 297, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9 and 780.1; the drug-induced psychosis codes 292.1, 292.11 and 292.12 appear only in the exclusion list, although the text says other stimulant use disorders with psychosis were included. The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and should be considered exploratory.

results.note: Numbers confirmed against Table 3 (4.49, 4.09 to 4.93; 5.07; 5.24; 5.53; 6.25, 5.42 to 7.20; p for trend 0.038 in the fifth (IR) column of the text extraction) and Findings 4th paragraph; arrests counted from the index date to the study end date (Statistics 1st paragraph). Editors' calculations recomputed: regression of 4.40, 4.80, 4.81, 4.84, 5.45 on 1 to 5 gives t = 3.56, df 3, p = 0.0377 (with the zero category p = 0.070; on log HRs p = 0.004, so only the five-rate regression reproduces the printed value); person-years per person 178,802/40,880 = 4.37 and 42,589/6,572 = 6.48. Conclusions 3rd paragraph (no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity) and 6th paragraph (police activity, comparison group may include people who use, more frequent use more likely arrested) match. One correction: the authors do not say arrests 'miss most use'; they say arrests do not capture all use and many people who use will never be detected or arrested. Role qualifies: right.
results.corrected_extracted: By number of arrests, counted from the index date to the end of the study, adjusted HRs: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93), two 5.07, three 5.24, four 5.53, five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20); p for trend 0.038, printed in the incidence-rate column, which a linear regression of the five category rates on the number of arrests reproduces (editors' calculation). Person-years per person rise from about 4.4 with one arrest to 6.5 with five or more (editors' calculation). The authors state that the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity, so dose dependence could not be asserted, that arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use (many people who use are never arrested), that the comparison group may include people who use amphetamines, and that people who use more often may be more likely to be arrested.
